newsitem.title: PERU: Peru army sweeps jungle as Tokyo urges rebel talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru army sweeps jungle as Tokyo urges rebel talks.

text.p: Tokyo looked to step up its efforts on Wednesday for a peaceful end to Lima's three-month hostage siege after Peru's army said it captured 38 jungle rebels from the Marxist movement holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home.

Japan's Vice Foreign Minister, Masahiko Komura -- in Lima for two days to press the government to push for fresh talks with the hostage-takers -- was set to leave later on Wednesday for Cuba to try to secure an offer of asylum.
Tokyo's envoy was due to fly on Thurday to the Dominican Republic, which was also believed to be willing to grant asylum to some of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

Cuban President Fidel Castro told Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori last month that the rebels could have asylum in Cuba. Following Fujimori's trip, the rebels told reporters they wanted to stay in Peru but said they reserved comment on the possibility of asylum in Cuba.
There was speculation that Komura's Caribbean trip was aimed at establishing legal mechanisms for any asylum for the rebels and arranging that some went to Cuba and others to the Dominican Republic.

The Peruvian military said on Tuesday the group of "MRTA terrorists" captured in its sweep planned to attack an army base in the town of Oxapampa, some 200 miles (325 kms) east of Lima. But villagers said the soldiers detained peasants unconnected to the MRTA.
They told TV station America Television the army killed one person and tortured others in the operation.
"They threw him, pulled him and he probably tried to escape and the (bullet) caught him," said Florencia Roldan, who said her husband, Fortunato Chipana, was shot and killed by soldiers on Feb. 25.

The army did not say when the suspected rebels were detained. As late as Sunday, however, the rebels said none of their members had been caught despite a major army offensive to flush them out of their jungle strongholds.

Comrade Alejandro, who identified himself as a member of the MRTA's high-command, told Reuters in a communication from the jungle, the army was deploying more than 500 soldiers to search for the group's military bases in Junin.
The senior rebel said the army had only detained villagers claiming they were MRTA members.
Last week, a leading Peruvian human rights group, APRODEH, said the whereabouts of four villagers in the area were unknown after an army operation March 9 led to the detention of 21 peasants.
The military, which earlier denied the sweep, said soldiers had respected human rights in its operation.
With the increased possibility of rebel-army clashes in the jungle, Komura met President Fujimori for two hours on Tuesday and urged him to move faster on peace talks to free the 72 hostages.
Since negotiations were put on hold last week, speculation has grown that Fujimori might try to storm the diplomatic compound.
"Mr. Komura expressed his desire for the discussions ... to be accelerated," Katsuyuki Tanaka, deputy director of Japan's special office in Lima, told reporters.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday morning, Komura said he asked Fujimori to respond to proposals by a three-man mediation panel, known as the guarantors commission, to resolve the standoff peacefully. He did not say what those proposals were.
"I asked President Fujimori to respond to efforts by the guarantors commission," Komura said through a translator.
